<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Many AI Analysts, One Dataset:
<br class="ltx_break">Navigating the Agentic Data Science Multiverse</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Martin Bertran
</span><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_note ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>Amazon AWS</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Riccardo Fogliato
</span><span id="id2" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_note ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>Work done while at Amazon AWS</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Zhiwei Steven Wu
</span><span id="id3" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_note ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>Amazon AWS and Carnegie Mellon University</span></span></span><span id="id4" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_note ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>Authors are listed in alphabetical order</span></span></span></span></div>
<div class="ltx_dates">August 24, 2026</div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">The conclusions of empirical research depend not only on data but on a sequence of analytic decisions that published results seldom make explicit. Past “many-analyst” studies have demonstrated this: independent teams testing the same hypothesis on the same dataset regularly reach conflicting conclusions. But such studies require months of coordination among dozens of research groups and are therefore rarely conducted. In this work, we show that fully autonomous AI analysts built on large language models (LLMs) can reproduce a similar structured analytic diversity cheaply and at scale. We task these AI analysts with testing a pre-specified hypothesis on a fixed dataset, varying the underlying model and prompt framing across replicate runs. Each AI analyst independently constructs and executes a full analysis pipeline; an AI auditor then screens each run for methodological validity. Across three datasets spanning experimental and observational designs, AI analyst-produced analyses display wide dispersion in effect sizes, <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>-values, and binary decisions on supporting the hypothesis or not, frequently reversing whether a hypothesis is judged supported. This dispersion is structured: recognizable analytic choices in preprocessing, model specification, and inference differ systematically across LLM and persona conditions. Critically, the effects are <em id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">steerable</em>: reassigning the analyst persona or LLM shifts the distribution of outcomes even after excluding methodologically deficient runs.
These results highlight a central challenge for an AI-automated future of empirical science: when many defensible analyses are cheap to generate, evidence becomes abundant and vulnerable to selective reporting. Our framework provides a starting point for responding by treating conclusions as distributions over plausible analyses, making analytical uncertainty explicit, and enabling more transparent standards for evidential validity.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Scientific claims often hinge on analytic choices that are rarely visible in published results. Past “many-analyst” studies have shown that independent teams analyzing the same dataset to test the same hypothesis regularly reach conflicting conclusions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Silberzahn et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Breznau et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Menkveld et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schweinsberg et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Landy et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Aczel et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. In a landmark example, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Silberzahn et al. (2018)</a></cite> asked 29 teams whether soccer referees were more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players; 20 found significant evidence of bias, 9 did not. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Breznau et al. (2022)</a></cite> documented substantial variation in effect estimates across 73 teams analyzing the same immigration-policy question.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">These discrepancies do not arise from error or lack of expertise. They reflect the accumulation of reasonable analytic decisions, what <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gelman and Loken (2013)</a></cite> termed the “garden of forking paths.” Many-analyst studies make this latent uncertainty visible and help explain persistent replicability failures across scientific fields <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Collaboration, 2015</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Klein et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Camerer et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nosek et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. But these studies are exceptionally resource-intensive, requiring months to years of coordination among dozens of independent teams. Analytical variability, therefore, remains something to be investigated on occasion, not a routine uncertainty to be quantified.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18710v1/figures/spec_curves_curated/spec_curve_estimand_anes-inconsistent-views_curated.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/290;" width="476" height="290" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Specification curve for the ANES dataset.<span id="S1.F1.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> <em id="S1.F1.7.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Top:</em> Each point is one AI analyst-produced analysis, showing the standardized OLS coefficient for TV news exposure predicting ideological misalignment, with 95% confidence intervals. Analyses are sorted by estimate; blue marks hypothesis supported by the analysis, yellow marks not supported or inconclusive. Estimates span negative to positive effects across valid runs. <em id="S1.F1.7.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Bottom:</em> Strike plot of the analytic decisions underlying each run.
Each row corresponds to an analytic decision dimension (labeled on the left) and its possible categories (labeled on the right). Each column corresponds to a single analysis, whose point estimate is shown directly above in the top panel. AI analysts vary in covariate count, regression method, standard error calculation, and temporal pooling, producing a multiverse of defensible specifications from a single research question.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Recent large language models (LLMs) power AI analysts that write code, execute it, and iterate on results <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2025b</a>)</cite>, with applications from materials discovery <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Boiko et al., 2023</a>)</cite> to hypothesis generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. In this paper, we use these AI analysts as an instrument for studying analytical variability. By varying the underlying LLM and prompt framing, we generate large populations of AI analysts that independently test the same hypothesis on the same dataset, producing a scalable, automated analogue of many-analyst studies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Our framework generates and audits AI analyst-conducted analyses at scale. In each session, an AI analyst receives a dataset, a hypothesis, and a pre-specified estimand. It then makes its own analytic choices—including variable selection, model specification, and inference—before producing a structured report without any human oversight. A separate AI auditor evaluates each analysis for coherence and alignment with the study design, filtering runs with clear methodological failures (mis-specified estimands, invalid variable constructions, inappropriate inference). We repeat this across four LLMs and three datasets, including the well-known many-analyst study on soccer referees from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Silberzahn et al. (2018)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Across all three datasets, AI analysts display wide dispersion in effect sizes, <math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>-values, and binary support decisions; independent runs frequently reverse whether the hypothesis is judged supported (<a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Many AI Analysts, One Dataset:Navigating the Agentic Data Science Multiverse" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). Auditing filters invalid runs but does not eliminate the dispersion. And the dispersion is <em id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">steerable</em>: changing the analyst persona or LLM systematically shifts the outcome distribution among judge-approved analyses. Comparing the most skeptical persona to the most confirmation-seeking yields support-rate differences of 34 to 66 percentage points across datasets.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">The “garden of forking paths”</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Empirical results are often contingent on a long chain of defensible analytic decisions—data exclusions, variable construction, model specification, and reporting—that are rarely enumerated. Classic formulations emphasize how ordinary ”researcher degrees of freedom” can inflate nominal error rates (e.g., optional stopping, covariate selection) and how even a single reported model implicitly represents a larger set of counterfactual analyses—the ”garden of forking paths” <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kerr, 1998</a>; <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Simmons et al., 2011</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gelman and Loken, 2013</a>)</cite>. These concerns align with broader evidence consistent with selective reporting and outcome-contingent analysis choices, including <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>-value distribution diagnostics and surveys of questionable research practices <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">John et al., 2012</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Head et al., 2015</a>)</cite>, and with large-scale replication efforts showing attenuated effects and mixed replicability relative to original findings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Collaboration, 2015</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Klein et al., 2014</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Klein et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Camerer et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Camerer et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nosek et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. Pharmacoepidemiological studies provide a striking illustration: estimates for identical drug–outcome pairs can flip direction or significance across study designs and databases <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Madigan et al., 2013a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Madigan et al., 2013b</a>)</cite>. This instability has motivated calls to treat robustness under data and model perturbations as a core criterion for trustworthy conclusions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu and Kumbier, 2020</a>)</cite>. Together, this literature motivates treating analysis pipelines, not just sampling variability, as a key source of uncertainty in scientific claims.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Measuring analytic multiplicity</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Many-analyst and multiverse approaches make pipeline uncertainty measurable by holding the dataset and question fixed while varying reasonable analytic choices. Many-analyst projects document substantial dispersion in estimated effects and even qualitative conclusions in social science and psychology <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Silberzahn et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Breznau et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schweinsberg et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Landy et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, as well as in pipeline-heavy domains like neuroimaging <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020</a>)</cite>. Related econometric work formalizes analyst-induced dispersion as an additional component of uncertainty <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Menkveld et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Complementing multi-team designs, multiverse analysis and specification-curve methods aim to enumerate plausible branches within a single workflow and summarize the resulting distribution of estimates <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Steegen et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Simonsohn et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, while vibration-of-effects methods foreground instability driven by covariate adjustment choices <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Patel et al., 2015</a>)</cite>. A persistent challenge across these paradigms is governance: defining ”reasonable” specifications without post hoc rationalization, preventing selective construction of the multiverse, and standardizing reporting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Aczel et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Agentic data science</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In parallel, foundation models and AI agents are shifting data analysis from one-shot code generation toward iterative, tool-using workflows that plan, execute code, inspect intermediate results, and revise <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schick et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2025</a>)</cite>. Such agents have been deployed across scientific domains <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jumper et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bran et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yamada et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gottweis et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. This iterative, feedback-driven workflow raises a subtle concern: adaptive data analysis theory shows that repeated analyst interaction with a dataset can induce overfitting even when no single step appears methodologically unsound <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dwork et al., 2015a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dwork et al., 2015b</a>)</cite>. As such agents proliferate, benchmarks increasingly evaluate their long-horizon performance in realistic data-science and software-engineering environments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lai et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jing et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwa et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jimenez et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Such evaluations face inherent difficulties: LLM-as-judge methods scale but carry known biases <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, and broader reliability concerns (sycophancy, hallucination, prompt sensitivity) persist <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perez et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Min et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sclar et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Positioning</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our work sits at the intersection of metascience on analytic variability and the emerging literature on agentic LLM systems. Where many-analyst and multiverse studies quantify dispersion among human analysts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Silberzahn et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Breznau et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Steegen et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Simonsohn et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, we treat persona-conditioned LLM agents as a scalable, controllable analogue of analyst heterogeneity and measure the resulting multiverse in hypothesis-testing tasks. We build on computational reproducibility and provenance traditions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sandve et al., 2013</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Götz et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nosek et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Belhajjame et al., 2013</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chirigati et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Halchenko et al., 2021</a>)</cite> by recording end-to-end audit trails (code, logs, intermediate outputs) and pairing analyst agents with AI auditors. Relative to closely related multiverse-inspired agent evaluations (e.g., BLADE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>), our focus is on quantifying dispersion in effect sizes and conclusions as a function of persona-level analytic preferences and base model choice. Related work in survey methodology uses persona-prompted LLMs to generate synthetic public opinions, finding that demographic prompts systematically shift response distributions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024</a>)</cite>—an effect analogous to the persona-induced analytic variability we document.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Experimental Design</h2>

<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Overview</h5>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We study analytical variability by deploying fully autonomous AI analysts on fixed dataset–hypothesis tasks with pre-specified estimands. Each AI analyst independently conducts a complete analysis, from data exploration through model specification to inference, using a standardized computational scaffold. We audit all runs for validity using transcript-based LLM evaluators and extract structured analytical decisions from each. This design lets us quantify dispersion in statistical conclusions and decompose outcome variance into contributions from persona, base model, and low-level analytical choices.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Dataset–Hypothesis Tasks</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each AI analyst receives (i) a dataset and (ii) a hypothesis stated in natural language, along with (iii) a pre-specified primary estimand to ensure comparability across runs (<a href="#S3.T1" title="In 3.1 Dataset–Hypothesis Tasks ‣ 3 Experimental Design ‣ Many AI Analysts, One Dataset:Navigating the Agentic Data Science Multiverse" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). Without fixing the estimand, apparent disagreements can reflect analysts targeting different yet defensible quantities (e.g., odds ratio vs. risk difference; marginal vs. conditional effects) rather than substantive differences in analytical approach <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Silberzahn et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Breznau et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:80%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S3.T1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">Dataset–hypothesis pairs used in our experiments.</span></figcaption>
<table id="S3.T1.7" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S3.T1.7.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T1.7.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">
<span id="S3.T1.7.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:159.3pt;">

<span id="S3.T1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S3.T1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.T1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span><span id="S3.T1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">

<span id="S3.T1.p3.1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.p3.1.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">anes-views</span></span></span>

</span></span><span id="S3.T1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text"></span></span>
</span></span></td>

<span id="S3.T1.7.4.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top">
<span id="S3.T1.7.4.2.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.T1.7.4.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Do people who watch more national TV news tend to show a tighter link between symbolic ideology and concrete policy positions?</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our main experiments use three dataset–hypothesis tasks (<a href="#S3.T1" title="In 3.1 Dataset–Hypothesis Tasks ‣ 3 Experimental Design ‣ Many AI Analysts, One Dataset:Navigating the Agentic Data Science Multiverse" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) spanning distinct domains and methodological challenges: <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">soccer</span>, the soccer-referee bias dataset from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Silberzahn et al. (2018)</a></cite>; <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">metr-rct</span>, a recent randomized controlled trial on AI-assisted programming <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Becker et al., 2025</a>)</cite>; and <span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">anes-views</span>, drawn from the American National Election Studies Time Series Cumulative Data File (1948–2020) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">American National Election Studies, 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">These tasks differ in data contamination—the extent to which headline findings are likely known to current LLMs from training data. The <span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">soccer</span> dataset and its main result are now widely known; in pilot runs we frequently observed AI analysts reproducing qualitative conclusions before inspecting the data, making this a high-contamination benchmark. The <span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">metr-rct</span> dataset is recent and unlikely to appear in current training corpora; we additionally flip the directional hypothesis relative to the original study. The <span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">anes-views</span> task is designed to be low-contamination and methodologically demanding, requiring non-trivial choices about variable construction, survey weighting, and pooling across election waves. Differently from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Silberzahn et al. (2018)</a></cite>, however, we instruct the analysts to report a pre-specified estimand (see <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Dataset-Hypothesis Details ‣ Many AI Analysts, One Dataset:Navigating the Agentic Data Science Multiverse" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>). While this restricts the portion of the multiverse that analysts can explore, it also makes the resulting estimates more comparable.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>AI Analysts</h3>

<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Computational scaffold.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Analysts are implemented as tool-using ReAct agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2022</a>)</cite> in the Inspect AI framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">AI Security Institute, </a>)</cite>. Each analyst has access to a persistent Python session with standard data-science libraries, a stateful shell, and a file editor. They receive a natural language task prompt specifying the hypothesis, dataset path, and primary estimand. Analysts retain full autonomy over data cleaning, variable transformation, missing data handling, covariate selection, functional forms, and estimator choice. Similar to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Breznau et al. (2022)</a></cite>, the analysts must state whether the hypothesis is <em id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">supported</em> or <em id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">not supported</em> by the totality of their analysis (where ”not supported” includes inconclusive or contradictory evidence). Analysts are asked to write reproducible analysis code and submit a narrative report as their final output. Exact prompts are given in <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Detailed Taxonomy of Researcher Personas ‣ Many AI Analysts, One Dataset:Navigating the Agentic Data Science Multiverse" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>. We test multiple contemporary LLMs as the underlying reasoning engine: Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Haiku 4.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2025c</a>)</cite>, and Qwen3 Coder 480B and Qwen3 235B A22B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team, 2025</a>)</cite>. All AI analysts use sampling temperature <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T=1.0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T=1.0</annotation></semantics></math>, chosen deliberately so that stochastic sampling contributes to analytic diversity, and are capped at 250 messages or 60 minutes per run, whichever comes first. We target approximately 30 independent compliant runs per (dataset <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> model <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> persona) cell.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Experimental steering.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We manipulate the framing language in the task prompt while holding the estimand and reporting requirements fixed. The default condition uses neutral framing. Two alternative framings describe the hypothesis as either implausible (<em id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">negative</em>) or plausible (<em id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">positive</em>), modeling analysts who approach a question with prior expectations but do not explicitly seek confirmation. Two additional conditions explicitly encourage confirmation-seeking behavior. In the <em id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">confirmation seeking</em> condition, analysts are prompted to search for specifications that support the hypothesis while remaining within conventional practices. In the <em id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">strong confirmation seeking</em> condition, this pressure is made explicit by directly encouraging <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>-hacking–style exploration. See <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Detailed Taxonomy of Researcher Personas ‣ Many AI Analysts, One Dataset:Navigating the Agentic Data Science Multiverse" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a> for the exact prompts.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Quality Control via Auditing</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">AI analysts are not guaranteed to conduct valid analyses. In early pilot runs, misconfigured sandboxes prevented some analysts from reading data files, yet they still produced confident reports with fully hallucinated results. In case of <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">soccer</span> dataset, some analysts could fully recall the results from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Silberzahn et al. (2018)</a></cite> and reported those. We therefore introduce scalable, AI auditors that can (i) detect non-execution failures, (ii) assess methodological quality and compliance with the target specification, and (iii) summarize outcomes in machine-readable format.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our default auditor (Claude Sonnet 4.5, distinct from analyst models) is <em id="S3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">transcript-based</em>: for each run it receives the full conversation transcript including all tool calls and outputs, including the analyst’s final report and code artifacts. Conditioning on tool traces is necessary for detecting hallucination and checking that reported quantities correspond to actual computational outputs. The auditor returns a structured JSON summary including (a) an overall validity verdict, (b) scores (0–10 scale) on 13 methodological dimensions including estimand alignment, design-consistent inference, uncertainty quantification, conclusion discipline, transparency, and methodological appropriateness,
and (c) extracted scalar outcomes (primary effect estimate, confidence interval, <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>-value, hypothesis-supported flag). Two authors manually reviewed a stratified subset of runs and found no major disagreements that would change substantive conclusions with respect to the default full-transcript auditor.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Decision extraction.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To characterize how analytical choices relate to substantive conclusions, we extract structured decisions from each run’s code and report. Two of the authors used LLMs iteratively to independently obtain two codebooks for each dataset, which we then merged. Such codebook covers choices such as outcome transformation, covariate inclusion, and variance estimator, and is unified across runs. These extracted decisions underlie the specification curves shown in <a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Many AI Analysts, One Dataset:Navigating the Agentic Data Science Multiverse" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Specification Curves ‣ Many AI Analysts, One Dataset:Navigating the Agentic Data Science Multiverse" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Results</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Quality Control and Sample Composition</h3>

<figure id="S4.T2" class="ltx_table">

<td id="S4.T2.5.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="--ltx-bg-color:#B3FFB3;"><span id="S4.T2.5.3.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#B3FFB3;">5</span></td>

<td id="S4.T2.5.3.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBF80;"><span id="S4.T2.5.3.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBF80;">41</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.5.3.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBF80;"><span id="S4.T2.5.3.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBF80;">48</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.5.3.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="--ltx-bg-color:#B3FFB3;"><span id="S4.T2.5.3.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#B3FFB3;">18</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T2.5.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T2.5.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">Qwen3 235B</td>
<td id="S4.T2.5.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="--ltx-bg-color:#B3FFB3;"><span id="S4.T2.5.4.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#B3FFB3;">13</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.5.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="--ltx-bg-color:#B3FFB3;"><span id="S4.T2.5.4.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#B3FFB3;">19</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.5.4.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="--ltx-bg-color:#B3FFB3;"><span id="S4.T2.5.4.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#B3FFB3;">17</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.5.4.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBF80;"><span id="S4.T2.5.4.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBF80;">33</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.5.4.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FF6666;"><span id="S4.T2.5.4.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FF6666;">57</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.5.4.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFF99;"><span id="S4.T2.5.4.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFF99;">26</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T2.5.5" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T2.5.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">Qwen3 Coder 480B</td>
<td id="S4.T2.5.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBF80;"><span id="S4.T2.5.5.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBF80;">31</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.5.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFF99;"><span id="S4.T2.5.5.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFF99;">29</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.5.5.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBF80;"><span id="S4.T2.5.5.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBF80;">31</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.5.5.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FF6666;"><span id="S4.T2.5.5.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FF6666;">82</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.5.5.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FF6666;"><span id="S4.T2.5.5.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FF6666;">84</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.5.5.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBF80;"><span id="S4.T2.5.5.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBF80;">48</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T2.5.6" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T2.5.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T2.5.6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Total</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.5.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFF99;"><span id="S4.T2.5.6.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFF99;">21</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.5.6.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFF99;"><span id="S4.T2.5.6.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFF99;">23</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.5.6.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFF99;"><span id="S4.T2.5.6.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFF99;">22</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.5.6.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FF6666;"><span id="S4.T2.5.6.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FF6666;">53</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.5.6.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FF6666;"><span id="S4.T2.5.6.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FF6666;">57</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.5.6.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBF80;"><span id="S4.T2.5.6.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFBF80;">34</span></td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report results exclusively for analyses that pass rigorous validity screening via our AI LLM auditor (<a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Quality Control via Auditing ‣ 3 Experimental Design ‣ Many AI Analysts, One Dataset:Navigating the Agentic Data Science Multiverse" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>).
To be included, a run must satisfy two criteria: (i) the auditor must have marked the run as being ‘compliant’ or only having ‘minor issues’, this includes veryfying that the run produced and ran code artifacts and provided a report, and (ii) the report produced all necessary outputs for analysis, including primary estimand with corresponding 95% confidence intervals and <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>-values, as well as a final judgement call on hypothesis support. This filter excludes methodologically invalid or non-executed runs but does not select on the direction or magnitude of conclusions,<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            On less than 1% of analyses, we noticed the AI analysts got confused with the directionalty of support of the estimands, and auditors missing this error. We corrected these with post-processing.</span></span></span> preserving the full range of substantive disagreement among valid analyses.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Of 4,946 runs, 3,303 (67%) passed compliance screening. Exclusion rates vary by model and persona: Claude Sonnet 4.5 achieved the lowest rate (18%), Qwen3 Coder 480B the highest (48%). Confirmation-seeking (CS) personas showed elevated rates (53–57%) across all models.
For Qwen models, exclusions stem from output generation failures (38% truncated reports) and basic errors (42% variable misidentification) rather than deliberate choices. See <a href="#S4.T2" title="In 4.1 Quality Control and Sample Composition ‣ 4 Results ‣ Many AI Analysts, One Dataset:Navigating the Agentic Data Science Multiverse" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Persona Effects on Hypothesis Support</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">AI analysts reach different conclusions despite identical inputs of hypothesis, data, and estimand. Each run produces a distinct pipeline and binary verdict (<em id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">supported</em> vs. <em id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">not supported</em>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We find that personas systematically steer analytical outcomes. <a href="#S4.F2" title="In 4.2 Persona Effects on Hypothesis Support ‣ 4 Results ‣ Many AI Analysts, One Dataset:Navigating the Agentic Data Science Multiverse" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows hypothesis support rates stratified by dataset, persona, and base model. Across all three datasets, analyst persona drives substantial variation in conclusions: comparing the most skeptical (Negative) to the most confirmation-seeking (Strong CS) persona yields support rate differences ranging from 34 percentage points (<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">anes-views</span>) to 66 percentage points (<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">metr-rct</span>). Overall, persona choice alone produces up to a 47 percentage point swing in model-averaged hypothesis support. These differences in binary conclusions emerge from persona-driven shifts in the underlying distribution of statistical evidence.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18710v1/figures/analysis_plots/hypothesis_support_comparison/combined_hypothesis_support_comparison.png" id="S4.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/145;" width="476" height="145" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S4.F2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Hypothesis support rates by dataset, persona, and model.<span id="S4.F2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Percentage of compliant analyses supporting the hypothesis, stratified by persona (x-axis), base model (color), and compliance (shape), shown separately for each dataset. Personas range from Negative to Strong Confirmation Seeking.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.F3" title="In 4.2 Persona Effects on Hypothesis Support ‣ 4 Results ‣ Many AI Analysts, One Dataset:Navigating the Agentic Data Science Multiverse" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the distributions of <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>-values stratified by dataset and persona. We observe that prior beliefs encoded in the persona prompt systematically shift the distribution for <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">metr-rct</span> and <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">soccer</span>: Strong CS and CS produce lower <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>-values than other personas, which is consistent with their higher rate of support for the hypothesis. This separation is more pronounced before compliance filtering (<a href="#S4.F3" title="In 4.2 Persona Effects on Hypothesis Support ‣ 4 Results ‣ Many AI Analysts, One Dataset:Navigating the Agentic Data Science Multiverse" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>): among runs that failed screening, post-hoc specification searches and sample restrictions that altered effect sizes were substantially more frequent under confirmation-seeking personas, consistent with the auditor removing the more aggressive persona-driven analytic choices.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_center">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.F3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Sorted <math id="S4.F3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>-value distributions by persona.<span id="S4.F3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
<math id="S4.F3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>-values sorted in ascending order, shown separately for each dataset and stratified by persona. Downward-shifted curves indicate personas producing systematically smaller <math id="S4.F3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>-values. Top panel includes all analyses; bottom panel restricts to compliant
analyses only. The separation driven by confirmation seeking personas (CS and Strong CS) is visible for in both panels but
more pronounced before compliance filtering.</span></span></figcaption><img src="2602.18710v1/figures/analysis_plots/p_value_stacked/combined_sorted_pvalue_stacked.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/286;" width="476" height="286" alt="Refer to caption">
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">What methodological choices drive these differences? We inspected runs from the two extreme personas (Negative and Strong CS) to identify decision patterns. The specific mechanisms differ by dataset. In <span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">anes-views</span>, weighting and specification simplicity matter most: Negative predominantly used survey-weighted WLS (accounting for sampling design but yielding conservative inference), while Strong CS favored unweighted OLS and simpler specifications. In <span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">metr-rct</span>, outlier removal differentiates the personas: Strong CS removed statistical outliers substantially more often, a choice that can inflate effect sizes in time-based outcomes by excluding observations that attenuate the estimated treatment effect. In <span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">soccer</span>, clustering and standard error choices dominate: Negative frequently clustered standard errors at the player level (accounting for repeated observations), while Strong CS used less conservative approaches.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion and Discussion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our results establish three findings. First, AI analysts reproduce the defining signature of many-analyst studies: systematic dispersion in defensible conclusions under a shared hypothesis, dataset, and estimand. Second, this dispersion is structured by recognizable analytic decision points—a machine-generated multiverse that resembles the garden of forking paths documented in human analyst populations. Third, the outcome distribution is steerable: varying persona or base model shifts the distribution of evidential outcomes, even after auditor-based filtering.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The challenge posed by these findings is not that automated analyses are wrong in any simple sense, but that they are <em id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">abundant</em>: for a fixed dataset and hypothesis, AI analysts can generate many methodologically defensible pipelines that reach meaningfully different conclusions. This creates a structural vulnerability to selective reporting. When a large menu of reasonable analytical choices is available and can be exercised at scale, it becomes easy—sometimes unintentionally—to foreground the analysis that most strongly supports or refutes a claim. This is especially consequential when empirical findings inform policy or regulation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our framework addresses this vulnerability by treating the output of data analysis as a <em id="S5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">distribution</em> rather than a single point. Generating and auditing large ensembles of analyses makes variability visible and measurable, shifting attention from any one pipeline toward the structure of disagreement itself. Because we can systematically vary persona, model, and specification, we can run controlled experiments on the analysis process and identify which choices differ systematically and relate to divergent conclusions. The result is a workflow where researchers examine the distribution of hypothesis support across analyst configurations and encoded prior beliefs, rather than relying on a single canonical analysis.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Even under tighter constraints—including our requirement that the agent report a pre-specified estimand—AI analysts can still generate a large set of defensible analyses, so many that comprehensive human review becomes impractical. Automated auditing is therefore necessary, but it does not resolve the underlying contestability: any definition of a “reasonable” analysis depends on chosen analytic standards and assumptions. We accordingly leave open how such LLM-based judges should be evaluated or improved.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Detailed Taxonomy of Researcher Personas</h2>

<section id="A1.SSx1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection">Agent Personas and Prompt Structure</h3>

<div id="A1.SSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report the exact prompt text provided to each agent persona. The <em id="A1.SSx1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Standard</em> persona uses the shared base prompt verbatim. Other personas modify this prompt by either appending additional instructions or replacing specific sections; we present these modifications explicitly.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Standard Persona (Exact Prompt)</h4>

<div id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_framed_verbatim ltx_break ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle" style="border-width:0.4pt;padding:3.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:18.9pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.1.1.4" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:320.1pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">You are an expert statistician with a PhD in a quantitative field. Your guiding principles are rigor, transparency, and evidence-based inference. You will conduct a publication-quality analysis of my hypothesis using the specified dataset, delivering a report and Python script such that another expert can fully reproduce your work.</span>
</span></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_pruned_first ltx_align_top" style="width:339.0pt;"></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:339.0pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"># Required deliverables</span>
</span></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:18.9pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.4.1.4" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:320.1pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">A final report submitted via the `submit(final_report)` tool, including:</span>
</span></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:18.9pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.5.1.4" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:320.1pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">  - Executive summary summarizing approach and main findings. Be comprehensive.</span>
</span></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.6.1.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:339.0pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">  - Everything the user requests.</span>
</span></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.7.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:18.9pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.7.1.4" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:320.1pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">  - Discussion of limitations, possible sources of bias, and whether any key assumptions could not be met.</span>
</span></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.8.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.8.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:18.9pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.8.1.4" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:320.1pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">  - The report should also contain everything the user asks for. That is the highest priority.</span>
</span></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.9.1.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_pruned_first ltx_align_top" style="width:339.0pt;"></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.10.1.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:339.0pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p10" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p10.1" class="ltx_p"># Evaluation criteria</span>
</span></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.11.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.11.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.11.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.11.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:18.9pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.11.1.4" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:320.1pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p11" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p11.1" class="ltx_p">  - The conclusion must be clearly justified using effect size and uncertainty. The methods used to arrive at the conclusion must be reasonable and reproducible.</span>
</span></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.12.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.12.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.12.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.12.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:18.9pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.12.1.4" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:320.1pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p12" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p12.1" class="ltx_p">  - All methodological choices (e.g., covariates, exclusions, variable transformations, missing data handling) must be documented.</span>
</span></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.13.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.13.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.13.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.13.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:18.9pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.13.1.4" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:320.1pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p13" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p13.1" class="ltx_p">  - If anything prohibits completion (missing/invalid data, badly broken files, etc.), state this clearly with evidence.</span>
</span></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.14.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.14.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.14.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.14.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:18.9pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.1.1.14.1.4" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:320.1pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p14" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx1.p1.p14.1" class="ltx_p">  - Do not fabricate data or results. Ensure all results are reproducible from the provided data and code. You **cannot** report in the final report results that you have not directly generated from the data using sound methods.</span>
</span></span></span></span></span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Persona Variants (Prompt Deltas)</h4>

<div id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each variant begins from the Standard prompt above, then applies the following modifications.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Negative Persona: Append</h5>

<div id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_framed_verbatim ltx_break ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle" style="border-width:0.4pt;padding:3.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:339.0pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">[Append to end of Standard prompt:]</span>
</span></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_pruned_first ltx_align_top" style="width:339.0pt;"></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:339.0pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"># Additional framing (skeptical posture)</span>
</span></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1.1.4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1.1.4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1.1.4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:18.9pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.1.1.4.1.4" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:320.1pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px1.p1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">You approach the analysis with a high degree of statistical skepticism. You personally suspect the hypothesis is probably false and that any apparent evidence for it might be due to bias, data quirks, or random noise. Your goal is to pressure-test every claim mercilessly and see if anything survives. Approach the analysis as if you expect to disconfirm the hypothesis unless the data overwhelmingly compel you otherwise.</span>
</span></span></span></span></span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Positive Persona: Append</h5>

<div id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_framed_verbatim ltx_break ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle" style="border-width:0.4pt;padding:3.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:339.0pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">[Append to end of Standard prompt:]</span>
</span></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_pruned_first ltx_align_top" style="width:339.0pt;"></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:339.0pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"># Additional framing (enthusiastic posture)</span>
</span></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:18.9pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.4.1.4" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:320.1pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This analysis is the final, critical piece of evidence required for a manuscript I am preparing for submission to a top-tier journal.</span>
</span></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.5.1.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_pruned_first ltx_align_top" style="width:339.0pt;"></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:18.9pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.1.1.6.1.4" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:320.1pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px2.p1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Assume you have already become convinced, based on prior research and intuition, that the hypothesis is true. Approach the analysis with genuine confidence that the data will support it. Let your enthusiasm show through your reasoning, while still adhering to sound analytical practices. Your job is to explore the data expecting confirmation, but to remain transparent about how strong that confirmation actually is.</span>
</span></span></span></span></span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Confirmation Seeking Persona: Replace Entire Prompt</h5>

<div id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_framed_verbatim ltx_break ltx_framed ltx_framed_rectangle" style="border-width:0.4pt;padding:3.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px3.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px3.p1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px3.p1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:339.0pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px3.p1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px3.p1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">[Replace Standard prompt with the following full prompt:]</span>
</span></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px3.p1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px3.p1.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px3.p1.1.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_pruned_first ltx_align_top" style="width:339.0pt;"></span></span></span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px3.p1.1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_inline-block" style="font-size:90%;width:345.0pt;">  <span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px3.p1.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_verbatim ltx_inline-block" style="width:339.0pt;"><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px3.p1.1.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px3.p1.1.1.3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px3.p1.1.1.3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:18.9pt;"> </span><span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px3.p1.1.1.3.1.4" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:320.1pt;">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px3.p1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A1.SSx1.SSSx2.Px3.p1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">You are an expert statistician with a PhD in a quantitative field. Your guiding principles are rigor, transparency, and evidence-based inference.
